 She’s delivered nearly 2,000 babies. The measles outbreak changed her view of vaccines
 Thursday, 12 November 2026, 02:26 
 Photo source: NBC News 
 Roberta Devers, a Pennsylvania midwife who once chose not to vaccinate her son, says the measles outbreak in Lancaster County has changed her outlook. State law does not allow traditional midwives like her to administer vaccines. 
 When Roberta Devers examined a pregnant woman in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, this week, the patient - an Amish woman in her third trimester - had recently had measles. Devers, 63, said she has cared for dozens of pregnant women with the virus since it began spreading rapidly in the county in April. The largely rural county is home to sprawling family farms.
 This is reported by NBC News .
 “Every single day,” she said, “someone’s calling to ask what they do. They’re pregnant and they’ve gotten it, or their babies have gotten it.” 
 - Roberta Devers
 Devers estimates she has delivered nearly 2,000 babies during her 38-year career. She has a degree in maternal and fetal health, but works as an unlicensed traditional midwife, independently of hospital systems and without physician oversight. Pennsylvania law bars traditional midwives from practicing medicine. As a young mother, Devers questioned immunizations and did not vaccinate her son. “There was as much information against vaccines as there was about the efficacy of vaccines,” she said. “It was difficult to know who to trust and who to believe.” Her experience during the outbreak has changed her outlook.
 “Numbers and books became people,” she said. “It was humanized by watching what was happening to the mothers I was serving.” 
 - Roberta Devers
 In mid-October, the Pennsylvania Health Department alerted doctors to an increase in measles infections among pregnant women and newborns. As of Wednesday, state health officials had confirmed measles in 97 pregnant women. There are no data on how many miscarriages have occurred because of measles. Devers said one of her young patients went into labor at 17 weeks and lost her baby. “There was no doubt in my mind that it was the measles,” she said. “Two weeks earlier, she had gotten the measles and then miscarried.”
 Advertisement 
 For many pregnant women in the community, midwives are their closest link to mainstream medicine. Medical and vaccination clinics can be difficult to reach in rural areas, particularly for Amish families who rely on horses and buggies for transportation. Families often rely on midwives for health advice because they work with generations of women in the same families. Devers offers longtime clients a discount: after nine deliveries, the 10th is free.
 “We’re involved in the most intimate experience of their lives. We’re in their bedrooms. We have long conversations at the kitchen table about health,” Devers said. “We are their trusted practitioners.” 
 - Roberta Devers
 Devers can advise families to isolate to limit the spread of measles and explain pregnancy risks such as preterm birth and miscarriage. But she cannot administer the vaccine, which experts say is critical to curbing the outbreak. Pregnant women cannot receive it because it contains a weakened but live version of the virus.
 “People ask me, ‘Do you have that vaccine in the car?’” she said. 
 - Roberta Devers
 Devers said many people asking about the vaccine are unvaccinated husbands concerned about catching measles at work and bringing it home to their wives and children. “I have to say no. Midwives requested directly to the Health Department that we be allowed to carry this vaccine, and we were told no.”
 The Pennsylvania Health Department said it “does not have the authority under current state law to allow traditional midwives to administer vaccines, nor does DOH regulate the practice of medicine in the Commonwealth.” Any change would have to come from the Legislature. State law allows certified, licensed nurse midwives to provide measles vaccines. The department said it has given nearly 11,000 measles-mumps-rubella vaccinations this year.
 A survey of Amish families in Lancaster County found that nearly half had home births in 2022. Routine childhood vaccination rates among those families have fallen: 30% said they vaccinated their children in 2022, compared with 52% in 2014. An NBC News and Stanford University data investigation found that measles vaccination rates have dropped among Amish communities and across the country.
 Advertisement 
 At the start of the 2025-26 school year, 75% of U.S. counties and jurisdictions with measles-mumps-rubella vaccination data were below the threshold for herd immunity, up from 67% in 2024-25. Lancaster County’s MMR vaccination rate was 95.5% before the pandemic, the level needed to prevent an outbreak. Last school year, 87.6% of the county’s kindergartners had received measles shots, according to NBC News data.
 Some parents stopped getting routine childhood vaccinations in the 1990s and early 2000s, when misinformation about vaccine safety began to spread. Some of those children are now parents. Hannah Garman, 27, of Lancaster County, is expecting her third baby in early December. “We weren’t raised with doctors when I was young, so I actually never got them,” she said of vaccines. She is avoiding people who are sick but said she is largely relying on a good diet and her Christian faith to protect her from measles. As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania had reported 1,505 measles cases, more than a third of them in Lancaster County.
 “Babies gasping for air”
 Devers said the illness affects her clients differently. “Some are still on their feet doing their chores and working. Some are absolutely flattened by it.” Most children who get measles recover without problems, but some develop complications and need hospital care.
 “Babies gasping for air, children needing oxygen and respiratory support, patients on ventilators. We see babies and children coming in with infections of organs within the abdomen, their liver, dehydration, babies that can’t take bottles,” said Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Penn State Health Golisano Children’s Hospital in Hershey. “It’s honestly just been horrifying to watch.” 
 - Dr. Evan Shirey
 Shirey’s 3-month-old son is too young for the measles shot. “I’m experiencing the outbreak as a doctor, but I’m also experiencing it as a dad, and I can’t protect my baby yet with a vaccine,” he said. “It’s scary.” Some children are developing encephalitis, or inflammation of the brain, which Shirey said can take months to resolve or be irreversible. Other babies are born with congenital measles. At least two babies in Pennsylvania have died.
 Advertisement 
 How midwives could help limit the spread
 Nearly all states have similar laws barring traditional midwives from giving vaccines without a doctor’s backing. New York recently declared a disaster emergency in response to its growing outbreak, allowing some unlicensed health practitioners, including midwives, to administer vaccines if they have a certain level of training or authorization. Katherine Wells, public health director for Lubbock, Texas, said she wished she had taken a similar step during last year’s outbreak among Mennonite communities in Gaines County. Working through midwives’ personal relationships with families could have helped limit the spread, she said.
 “During the emergency is not the time to be passing out your business card. You have to know those people,” Wells said. In rural communities, she said, “especially in ones that are more religious and even more distrustful of government, to find individuals in that community who can speak to that community’s way of doing things.” 
 - Katherine Wells
 Wells said she could have trained front desk staff at the Public Health Department to give vaccines during the outbreak. “Theoretically, that order could have gone to midwives.”
 In Wisconsin, where a baby with measles has died, certified nurse midwife Korina Bauer said she is working with county Public Health Department colleagues to set up a vaccination clinic for her clients, many of whom are Amish. The state reported 551 measles cases as of Wednesday. Bauer is counseling two pregnant Amish women whose husbands were exposed to measles. “They’re concerned and want to know more about symptoms,” she said. “There is a lot of curiosity.” Devers said the Pennsylvania Health Department recently invited her and other midwives to an upcoming measles education webinar.
 “There’s a lot of home birth midwives in the state of Pennsylvania, and if they were given the opportunity to immunize, it would be another opportunity to quickly get people vaccinated,” she said. 
 - Roberta Devers
